entries.contrast: Always capitalized. The collective is Americans rather than ✗ the American; the the + adjective pattern belongs to the -ish and -ese groups.

entries.contrast: Note that English uses one word where Russian distinguishes русский (ethnic) and россиянин (citizen). Context alone carries that difference in English.

senses.head: A person from Israel
examples: Two Israelis were on the panel.

entries.agreement: plural verb — Israelis serve in the military
entries.contrast: The -i nationality words take a plain -s: Israelis, Iraqis, Pakistanis, Saudis, Yemenis. Distinguish Israeli (a citizen of Israel) from Israelite (an ancient Hebrew) and Jewish (a religion and ethnicity) — three different words.

entries.meaning: A person from Japan; the language; also the adjective.
examples: Two Japanese were staying at the hotel.

senses.head: A person from Japan
examples: Two Japanese were staying at the hotel.
She's a Japanese student at the university.

senses.head: The language
examples: He reads Japanese but can't speak it.
Japanese uses three writing systems at once.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the Japanese are famously polite
entries.variants: a Japanese person is now preferred over the bare noun a Japanese
entries.contrast: ✗ Japaneses is always wrong. The singular noun — a Japanese — is grammatical but sounds dated and slightly impersonal in modern American English; say a Japanese person, a Japanese woman, a Japanese colleague. The collective the Japanese is perfectly normal.

senses.head: The language

entries.agreement: plural verb — the Chinese have a long tradition of it
entries.variants: a Chinese person is preferred over the bare noun
entries.contrast: ✗ Chineses is always wrong. Note that Chinese covers several distinct spoken languages — Mandarin, Cantonese — which share a writing system.

senses.head: A person from Switzerland

senses.head: As an adjective

entries.agreement: plural verb — the Swiss are famously neutral
entries.contrast: ✗ Swisses is wrong. Switzerland has four national languages, so Swiss names a nationality, never a language — ✗ she speaks Swiss is wrong; say Swiss German or French.

senses.head: The people of England

He's an Englishman married to a Scot.

entries.plural: the English (collective) · for individuals: Englishmen, English people, Britons
entries.countability: the adjective is not a countable noun for a person
entries.agreement: plural verb — the English drink a lot of tea
entries.contrast: ✗ An English and ✗ two Englishes are both wrong for people. Say an Englishman, an English person, or a Briton. Note also that English and British are not synonyms: English means from England, British from the United Kingdom, which includes Scotland and Wales.

entries.plural: the Dutch (collective) · for individuals: Dutchmen, Dutch people
entries.countability: the adjective is not a countable noun for a person
entries.agreement: plural verb — the Dutch are the tallest people in Europe
entries.contrast: ✗ A Dutch and ✗ two Dutches are wrong. The country is the Netherlands; Holland is strictly only two of its provinces, though it is widely used for the whole. The people are the Dutch, never ✗ the Netherlanders in ordinary speech.

entries.contrast: The pronunciation is the trap: the nationality Polish is POH-lish with a long o, while the unrelated noun polish meaning shine is PAH-lish with a short one. The noun for a person is a Pole, and ✗ a Polish is wrong.
